text: Chapter twenty-five, the real-time gaming leaderboard. Let's see how it works in four minutes.

Start with a relational database: one row per player, one column for the score. To get the top ten, you sort by score. Without a good index, that means scanning and sorting every row. Finding a player in the middle is worse: you have to count everyone ahead of them. With millions of players, that's expensive on every request.

A Redis sorted set solves this by keeping data in order all the time. Underneath, a hash table maps member to score, and a skip list keeps members sorted by score. A skip list is a sorted linked list with sparse index layers on top: take big jumps first, then small steps. In the book's example with sixty-four nodes, a plain list takes sixty-two steps. A skip list takes about eleven.

Four commands cover daily use. ZADD inserts a member or sets its score. ZINCRBY adds to a score. ZREVRANGE reads a range of ranks, highest first. ZREVRANK returns one member's position. Updates and lookups are logarithmic. A range read is logarithmic, plus the number of items returned.

When a player wins a match, we send one ZINCRBY: add one point to mary1934. Her entry follows the index to its new position, passes the player above her, and moves up one place. Everyone else shifts down automatically. Nothing gets re-sorted.
To get the top ten, use ZREVRANGE from zero to nine, with scores. The set is already ordered, so Redis just reads ten entries by position. No scan, no sort.

To show nearby players, first ask ZREVRANK for mary1934's position. In the book it's three hundred sixty-one, counting from zero. Then fetch four players on each side: positions three fifty-seven through three sixty-five, both ends included. If she's near the top, clamp the start at zero.

The competition runs monthly. Each month gets its own key, such as leaderboard underscore feb underscore twenty twenty-one. Every score update and every query uses that key. At month end, the old board is archived to historical storage, and the new month starts with an empty board.

Now scale. With five million daily active users, storage is about six hundred fifty megabytes, and peak load is twenty-five hundred updates per second. One Redis handles that. But at five hundred million users, it's sixty-five gigabytes and two hundred fifty thousand updates per second. You must shard. The book says ten times, but it's actually a hundred.

The first option is sharding by score range, say nine hundred to a thousand points on one shard. The top ten comes from the highest shard. A player's global rank is their position within the shard, plus the number of players on higher shards. The cost: when a score crosses a boundary, you must move the entry and update the routing.

The second option is sharding by hash of the player. For the global top ten, take each shard's top ten and merge them. If you're not in your shard's top ten, you can't be in the global top ten. The cost: more shards mean wider fan-out, and a personal rank means asking every shard. That's why the book prefers fixed score ranges.
To sum up. A sorted set makes ranks move with scores. A monthly key gives each season its own board. And sharding is a trade-off between merging the top ten and finding a personal rank.
